newsitem.title: UK: Malaysian PM's forex complaint rebuffed in London.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian PM's forex complaint rebuffed in London.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohammed blamed "rogue speculators" on Thursday for unjustly attacking ailing Asian currencies, but the response from London -- the world's biggest forex centre -- was that there's no smoke without fire.
"You're not able to speculate that successfully if there isn't some substance to your speculation," said Nick Douch, corporate risk adviser at BZW.

The Thai baht slumped to a record low in the latest Southeast Asian rout on Thursday, while Malaysia's ringgit touched its weakest level in more than three years and the Singapore dollar dived to a 33-month low.

Mahathir, opening the 30th foreign ministerial meetings of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN), spoke of a "well-planned effort to undermine the economies of all the ASEAN countries by destabilising their currencies".
But analysts said the market was simply sniffing out a money-making opportunity, not working to a cunning plan. That implied underlying tensions, they insisted.
"There is an element of truth in what Mahathir says but it should not blind monetary authorities to the problems that enabled speculators to be successful," said Douch.

The failure of the Thai authorities to prevent an effective devaluation of the baht has stoked concerns about the stability of many southeast Asian markets, which have attracted heavy inflows of foreign capital in recent years, analysts said.
Prime victims of speculative attack have been countries running current account deficits. A loss of investor confidence could dry up the inward capital flows they rely on.
Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan in London, said institutional investors were reducing their exposure in response to the volatile forex climate.
On top of that, domestic exporters and banks, short of foreign currencies, were covering their borrowings.
"It certainly isn't only naughty speculators," said Persaud.
Where Mahathir may have more of a point is in his assertion that regional central banks could improve their coordination to defend their currencies, analysts said.
Mahathir did not spell out how monetary authorities might cooperate better, but he said existing arrangements were not sufficient or effective to tackle the kind of situation currently at play.
"Where Mahathir is right is in talking about greater cooperation, because successful intervention is all about power," said BZW's Douch.
Analysts warned, though, that cooperation would have to extend further than concerted intervention -- though even that would clearly be more effective than unilateral action.

Thailand and Singapore intervened jointly in currency markets in May when the baht came under heavy attack. The Thai central bank has bilateral pacts with nations including China, Japan, Malaysia and Australia, designed to help stabilise currencies in emergencies.
Countries needed to discuss subjects such as currency regimes and the choice of base to which they should tie their currency, analysts suggested.

Nations which had weighted their currencies too heavily in U.S. dollars, for example, had suffered as the dollar powered higher since they had become too uncompetitive against non-dollar-based currencies.
For now, the southeast Asian countries will simply have to come to terms with the decline in their currencies, said Chris Tinker, chief economist at Standard Chartered here.
"This regional realignment is a reality," said Tinker. "We've got to get on with accepting it, rather than pointing the finger and saying it's speculators."
